title: Pathways to Information: The Tricks of the Trade or the Trade Itself?
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: In the second part of her series, Janetos tests Daniel Willingham's claim that reading comprehension strategies are a "bag of tricks" that are easy to learn and need little practice. From her work with struggling and dyslexic young readers, she argues that strategy instruction is neither easy nor brief for students who lack the decoding threshold, language experience or engagement. She distinguishes learning, practising and applying strategies, and wonders whether practice fails when done on disconnected passages, like shooting baskets rather than playing basketball. Drawing on Natalie Wexler, Shanahan, Kelly Cartwright and Pondiscio, she settles on a middle ground in which strategy instruction directly tackles the language of complex, knowledge-rich text.
points: Willingham's findings may underestimate the benefit of strategies, since only students who can decode and do not yet know the strategy gain from teaching.
The decoding threshold means comprehension support will not help children who cannot yet recognise words fluently.
Janetos separates learning, practising and applying a strategy, arguing that each application is also further practice.
Strategy practice on random, disconnected passages may be why extended practice seems ineffective, which makes knowledge-building texts the better setting.
The proposed middle ground teaches strategies through the language of complex text rather than choosing between strategies and knowledge.
quotes: It appears that reading strategies do not build reading skill, but rather are a bag of tricks that can indirectly improve comprehension. These tricks are easy to learn and require little practice, but students must be able to decode fluently before these strategies can be effective.

I want to emphasize, based on experience working with hundreds of these three types of students, that—yes—most definitely yes—the studies may well underestimate how much reading strategies actually help. All the more reason to teach them and practice applying them.

This is why I had to provide my third-graders who lacked sufficient decoding skills additional decoding support in small groups, along with providing them whole-group strategy instruction to be applied to grade-level text, with the hope that once the decoding threshold was crossed, the strategy would be waiting for them on the other side.
Or—maybe the ineffectiveness of extensive practice is related to practicing a comprehension strategy on random, disconnected passages—like practicing shooting baskets rather than playing basketball.

Similarly, you can’t just immerse students in knowledge-rich texts and expect them to absorb all the information. The middle ground involves accessing complex text through strategy instruction that directly tackles the language in that text in all its glory—and guises.

I wish I shared Willingham’s glee over how easy it is to learn strategies. Based on my experiences, I believe we need to distinguish between learning strategies, practicing strategies, and applying strategies. Each time a student is asked to apply a strategy, they are also practicing it and becoming more adept at utilizing it.
